# What the Septuagint's word meant


The Jews who translated Isaiah into Greek, before Christ, wrote παρθένος, read
as "virgin". That translation, the Septuagint, is the one Matthew quotes.
Doesn't it settle the question?

The argument is old. Irenaeus makes it against Theodotion and Aquila: the verse
"was interpreted into Greek by the Jews themselves, much before the period of
our Lord's advent, that there might remain no suspicion that perchance the Jews,
complying with our humour, did put this interpretation upon these words"
(*Against Heresies* III.21.1). It is encoded here at full strength, and three
things are asked of it, one result each.

**What it rests on.** Take away the claim that παρθένος, in the translator's
Greek, means a virgin, and the Septuagint no longer shows that its translator
read the woman as one (`parthenos_is_load_bearing`). Everything turns on that
word, and whether it means "virgin" there is exactly what the sources dispute.
Rico and Gentry hold that it does "whenever it appears in Semitic Koine Greek",
and Bratcher agrees. Wegner, Rhodea and Meade hold that in the translator's day
it still meant a young woman, as it does of Dinah after Shechem has lain with
her (Genesis 34:3), and Walton that the translator's choice of it "is not
necessarily betraying an interpretation as virgin". Wegner and Walton grant that
by the New Testament the word meant "virgin"; Meade and Davidson put that sense
down to Christian use. The dispute is over the translator's day, two or three
centuries before Matthew. The Greek Pentateuch's laws use the word where
virginity is the point, and its law of the seduced παρθένος reads Genesis 34:3
itself otherwise: the woman a man has lain with is still the law's παρθένος, and
owed "the bride-price of virgins" (Exodus 22:15–16). This chapter weighs all
five, below, and the Septuagint's witness prevails, with Rico and Gentry, the
laws and that reading of Genesis 34:3; Wegner cannot be defended
(`septuagint_prevails_over_wegner`). The verdict turns on one rating, the status
reading's step, `plausible` on the readers found.

**What it would show, if the word means "virgin".** How one early reader read
Isaiah: a Jewish translator, before Christ, read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin, so
reading her so is no Christian invention. It would not show what Isaiah's own word
means without a further step, rated `disputed`
(`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`). A translator can render the woman
described rather than the word. The translator of Genesis wrote παρθένος for the
עַלְמָה Rebekah (24:43), whom the story has already called a virgin (24:16): a
rendering "historically correct — since Rebekah was a virgin", Bratcher says,
that "does not precisely translate the Hebrew" (113). Elsewhere the Septuagint's
translators, of other books than Isaiah, render עַלְמָה with νεᾶνις, "young
woman", four times. That is how this argument's referential strand already reads
the versions.

**What it leaves open, even then.** The Greek says the virgin *shall* be with
child. A woman who is a virgin when the sign is given and conceives later by a
man fits those words as well as a virgin who conceives as a virgin does
(`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`). That is not only a rival's reading.
Bratcher, who holds that παρθένος "definitely means 'virgin' in the LXX" (113),
reads the Greek of 7:14 so: "a young woman, at that time virgin, would in the
normal way marry and bear a child" (115), "the most reasonable explanation"
(116). So the Septuagint, granted every word, does not by itself say that the
conception was without a man. Justin and
Irenaeus read it so, from the promise of a sign (`signLine`, weighed in the chapter
[Was the woman already pregnant?](wegner.md)); the word alone does not.

## The word weighed against its rivals


The Septuagint's witness rests on one claim, that παρθένος, in its
translator's Greek, means a virgin. Here that claim is weighed against its
rival. Six positions meet:

- **The Septuagint as a witness** (Irenaeus): Jews translated Isaiah before
  Christ and wrote a word that means a virgin, so they read the woman as one.
- **Wegner on παρθένος** (with Rhodea and Meade): in the Septuagint's day the
  word meant a young woman of marriageable age, and the sense "virgin" came
  later. Genesis 34:3 calls Dinah a παρθένος after Shechem has lain with her.
- **Rico and Gentry's case from usage**: παρθένος means a virgin "whenever it
  appears in Semitic Koine Greek", or the Jewish objection to it — Trypho's, and
  the Three's νεᾶνις — would have had no point. The library adds a ground of its
  own, encoded with theirs: the Greek Isaiah uses the word elsewhere only for
  בְּתוּלָה.
- **The case from the laws** (Bratcher's): the Greek Pentateuch, the corpus
  Genesis 34:3 comes from, uses the word in two laws where virginity is the
  point. The high priest marries a παρθένος — "a woman in her virginity", in the
  Hebrew — and not a widow, a woman put away, a defiled woman or a harlot
  (Leviticus 21:13–14). A bride without τὰ παρθένια, the tokens of virginity,
  dies for playing the harlot (Deuteronomy 22:13–21).
- **The status reading of Genesis 34:3**: Wegner's counterexample read under
  the law of the seduced παρθένος. The Greek Exodus still calls the woman a man
  has lain with a παρθένος, and has him pay "the bride-price of virgins"
  (22:15–16); Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act in that law's words. So at 34:3 the
  word names Dinah by the standing he took from her, in the sense "virgin".
- **Miller from Genesis 34:3**: "In one passage, this term refers to a rape
  victim after she has been attacked" (*Born Divine*). The word is said there of
  a woman no longer a virgin, so it did not by itself connote virginity, and the
  laws' virginity is the context's. His case as the texts leave it: his other
  example, Joel 1:8, is struck, because the Greek reads otherwise (below,
  under "a dissent, with what the texts refute struck").

## What this dispute does not decide

It is about a Greek word. It is not about the virgin birth, and not about
whether Isaiah 7:14 is fulfilled in Christ. That is weighed in `Dispute`, where
the scriptural reading prevails once the replies are heard
(`scriptural_reading_prevails_once_replies_are_heard`) and the critical denial
of the prediction belongs to no position that can be defended
(`critical_denial_indefensible`). That shows that the case against the
prediction does not survive the replies, on those premises and ratings; it does
not prove the prediction. And it needs neither side's claim about παρθένος.

Nor does it weigh Matthew's own reading of the word, from his quotation of it of
Mary. That is weighed in the chapter [Matthew's reading of the word](matthew.md), under each
standard.

Nor is it a dispute between believers and unbelievers. Wegner and Rhodea write
as evangelicals. Wegner holds that Isaiah 7:14 is used in Matthew "to refer to
Mary, who was indeed a virgin", the "only virgin birth in the Bible" (483).
Rhodea turns the weak sense of the word into an argument that Matthew did not
invent the virginal conception to fit Isaiah: neither the Hebrew nor the Greek
demands it, so Isaiah gave him no reason to (76).

## What the claims say, and how they are joined

The claims about the word are claims about its senses. Rico and Gentry's,
encoded, is that "virgin" is a sense of παρθένος in the Septuagint's Greek;
they say more, "whenever it appears". Wegner's is that the word meant "young
woman" there, and did not yet have the sense "virgin". Two senses of one word do
not exclude each other, so the two claims contradict each other only through
Wegner's "not yet": the library's account of what each claim means finds that
they cannot both be true (`TestimonyArguments.Meanings.BornOfAVirgin.joins`).

The laws are joined the same way. The case from the laws concludes that the
word has the sense "virgin" in two passages of the Septuagint. A sense a word
has in one passage of a text is a sense it has in that text's usage as a whole
(`Testimony.Ontology.Usage`): a definition of terms, not a reading of any text.
So the laws' sense, if it holds, makes "virgin" one of the word's senses in the
Septuagint's Greek. That is the claim encoded for Rico and Gentry, and the
witness's ground, and it excludes Wegner's "not yet 'virgin'". It does not say
which sense the translator of Isaiah used at 7:14; that move is the witness's
own step. Nor does the definition count a word used *of* a virgin as meaning
"virgin": a thousand uses of "fiancée" of virgins, Walton observes, would not
make it mean "virgin" (292). The laws count only because their contexts turn on
the sense.

Every party holds these joins, and each attack below is computed with them. In
the names of the results, *drift* is Wegner's case that the word's sense
shifted.

## How to read the verdicts

- **Defeats.** One position contradicts another, and the attack survives the
  ratings. An attack on a premise succeeds unless that premise is rated higher
  than the attacker's weakest link. An attack on a conclusion, or on a claim
  derived on the way, succeeds unless the attacked position is the stronger of
  the two. A defeat that runs both ways is a *standoff*.
- **Weakest link.** A position is only as strong as its least-supported premise
  or step. Four parties here rest on something rated `disputed`, the lowest
  rating. The status reading rests on a step rated `plausible`, one above, and
  so it outranks Wegner.
- **Prevails.** Accepted however every standoff is resolved.
- **A resolution.** A largest set of positions, none of which defeats another,
  that answers every attack on its members, itself or through an ally. A
  position in some resolution can be defended; one left out of some resolution
  is not forced — which is not the same as false.

## What the solver computed

Six standoffs, three with Wegner and three with Miller; one defeat of each by
the status reading, which neither can return; and nothing else
(`septuagintDispute_defeats`, all thirty-six pairs):

- **Wegner and the witness.** What Wegner holds denies the witness's ground that
  "virgin" is a sense of the word; what the witness holds denies his
  conclusion.
- **Wegner and Rico and Gentry.** Each concludes what the other's conclusion
  rules out.
- **Wegner and the laws.** The laws' sense excludes his "not yet 'virgin'", and
  his conclusion excludes theirs.
- **The status reading defeats Wegner.** Its sense "virgin" at Genesis 34:3
  excludes his "not yet 'virgin'". He attacks it back, by the same exclusion,
  and the attack fails: he is weaker than it
  (`drift_does_not_defeat_dinah`).
- **Miller and the witness, Rico and Gentry, and the laws.** His thesis, that the
  word did not by itself connote virginity, denies each of their senses, and
  each of them denies it; his conclusion and the laws' contradict each other
  outright.
- **The status reading defeats Miller.** Its sense "virgin" at 34:3 excludes his
  premise that the noun describes Dinah as she then was, and his thesis. He
  attacks it back and fails, for the same reason as Wegner. Miller and Wegner
  do not attack each other: Wegner's claim entails Miller's thesis.

The witness, Rico and Gentry, the laws and the status reading do not attack one
another. They stand together (`septuagint_stands_with_the_usage`). Rico and Gentry lend the witness
its contested ground: their conclusion is that ground, word for word. The laws
reach the same ground through the definition, so the library draws no support
from them, though they lead to the same place.

**The Septuagint's side prevails** (`septuagint_prevails_over_wegner`). Nothing
defeats the status reading, so it is accepted first. It defeats Wegner and
Miller, the only parties that defeat the witness, Rico and Gentry or the laws,
so all three are accepted with it. Neither Wegner nor Miller belongs to any
position that can be defended (`drift_indefensible`, `miller_indefensible`).
Miller's defeat overrules his dissent from the laws' step, so that the step
stands at its cited `wellSupported` (`Dispute.Miller`); this dispute weighs the
step at `disputed`, its floor, so the overruling does not lean on the rating it
lets stand. That is a verdict on these premises and these ratings,
and it turns on one of them, the status reading's step: see below.

## Where the evidence lies

The tie is a tie of ratings, and the ratings count dissenters, not evidence.
What each side brings is not alike, and a reader should see it.

For "virgin" as a sense of the word in the Septuagint's Greek:

- **The Greek Pentateuch's own usage.** Every בְּתוּלָה and בְּתוּלִים in the Hebrew
  Pentateuch — fifteen words in fourteen verses — has a παρθεν- word in the
  Greek, and its laws use the word where virginity is the point (read from
  Rahlfs's text and the Masoretic). Across the whole Septuagint, Bratcher counts
  παρθένος for בְּתוּלָה forty-five times out of fifty-two (113).
- **The lexica on the laws.** LSJ glosses τὰ παρθένια "signs of virginity", from
  Deuteronomy 22 (1339); Muraoka, "tokens of virginity" (535); LEH, "signs
  pertaining to virginity, virginity". LEH glosses παρθένος itself "virgin"
  first.
- **Readers who hold the sense, whatever they make of the prophecy.** Rico and
  Gentry; Bratcher, for whom the word "definitely means 'virgin' in the LXX"
  (113), though he reads 7:14 of a woman then a virgin who conceives "in the
  normal way" (115); and Delling, for whom the Septuagint's usage at 7:14
  demands "no more than the sense of a 'woman untouched by a man up to the
  moment of the conception'" (as Rhodea quotes him, 67 n. 42): a virgin until
  then, whatever followed. Rhodea, who follows Wegner, still writes that
  παρθένος "more properly means 'virgin'" (67), and holds that in the Septuagint
  it "need not refer to a virgo intacta".

For "young woman, and not yet 'virgin'":

- **Early Greek usage.** Early Greek had both senses. LSJ gives "maiden, girl",
  "virgin, opp. γυνή", and "of unmarried women who are not virgins" (1339);
  BDAG gives the general use "of a young woman of marriageable age, w. or
  without focus on virginity" from Homer on (777), and the sense "virgin" in the
  New Testament and the early Christian writings. Every side grants it.
- **Genesis 34:3**, one verse with the word twice, which every side grants:
  what the Greek reads. How it is read is the status reading's question.
- **Muraoka's lexicon**, which glosses παρθένος "young woman", lists Genesis 34:3,
  "so called just after having been raped", and marks "virginity stressed (?)"
  in the laws of Deuteronomy 22 (535).
- **Readers.** Wegner, Rhodea, Meade, Davidson and Miller; Walton doubts the
  virgin sense, citing Brown for the word's broader sense (293 n. 15). Brown
  himself holds that the translator chose "a deliberate preference for
  understanding the young woman of Isa 7:14 as a virgin" (*Birth of the Messiah*
  148): a claim about how the translator read the woman, not about the word.

None of this moves a rating. The solver weighs who contests a claim, not how
much evidence each side brings. But it does show what the tie is: between the
broader sense of early Greek, with one passage of the Septuagint, read by one
side as the rule; and the Septuagint's usage at large, read by the other as the
rule, with that passage the exception.

## What the ratings decide

**The verdict turns on the status reading's step**, from the law of the seduced
παρθένος and the law's words in Genesis 34 to the sense of the word at 34:3. It
is rated `plausible` (`dinahLine` gives the reasons in full). No cited reader
grants its grounds and denies its conclusion. Wegner, Rhodea, Meade, Rico and
Gentry and Bratcher read 34:3 as said of a woman no longer a virgin, but none
takes up Exodus 22:15–16 or the law's words in Genesis 34. Frymer-Kensky reads
the law and the story together, as the step does, from the Hebrew (80, 91). No
reader has been found who makes the status reading of the Greek. It is built
here from the texts, and that is why it is rated no higher.

Rated `disputed`, as it was first encoded, the status reading would stand off
with Wegner like the other three, nothing would prevail, and the dispute would
have two resolutions: the Septuagint's side, and Wegner alone. That was
computed, before the step's rating was audited. A reader of the Greek Genesis
who has the law before him and still reads 34:3 of a woman no longer a virgin
would bring it back. Wevers's *Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis* and Harl's
*La Genèse* have not been read.

**Wegner's step**, from the older usage and Genesis 34:3 to the Septuagint's
sense, is rated `disputed`, the lowest rating. Rico and Gentry, and Bratcher,
grant all its grounds and deny its conclusion: to Rico and Gentry, Genesis 34:3
is "the exception that proves the rule", an archaism of the Greek Pentateuch
(18, 21); to Bratcher, it is "surprising" (113). The higher ratings belong to
the grounds, not the step: that early Greek used παρθένος of a young woman (well
supported), that the Greek of Genesis 34:3 calls Dinah one (`consensus`), and
that the noun there describes her as she then was (well supported). That last
ground is Wegner's reading of the verse, not the text; every reader on record
who takes up the verse holds it, and only the status reading denies it. Neither
side's grounds say what the word meant at Isaiah 7:14.

**The other three steps**, Rico and Gentry's from the Jewish objection, the
laws' from what the two laws read, and the witness's own ground, are each
`disputed`, and the verdict does not need any of them raised.

- **Rico and Gentry's step.** It is `disputed` because Davidson (1899) and Meade
  (2013) grant the objection and read it the other way: the revisers wrote
  νεᾶνις against a sense Christians had put on the word, not one its translator
  gave it.
- **The laws' step** (`laws_rest_on_their_inference`). It is `disputed` on one
  reader. Miller grants that the laws require virgins, and holds that the
  virginity "has to be inferred from the context": "parthenos in the Septuagint
  did not by itself connote what we mean by virginity". Of what he says of the
  Greek, the young widow he finds at Joel 1:8 is not there in the Greek, which
  calls her a bride; the translators did not "consistently" use the word for
  עַלְמָה; and Genesis 34:3 is what the status reading reads otherwise. His point
  that the Greek adds "who has not known a man" where virginity matters
  (Genesis 24:16) translates a clause the Hebrew already has. The rating rests
  on him all the same. The Joel 1:8 example is struck, because the text refutes
  it, and his dissent still stands on Genesis 34:3, which the Greek reads as he
  says (`Dispute.Miller`).
- **The witness's own ground**, that "virgin" is a sense of the word, cited
  `disputed` because Wegner, Walton, Rhodea and Meade contest it.

The dissents on these steps are brief on both sides. Davidson hedges his account
of the Three with a "possibly", though not his account of the word; Meade's is a
blog comment revising his own earlier view. The ratings weigh none of this.

## A dissent, with what the texts refute struck


The laws' step (`lawsLine`) is rated `disputed` on one reader, Robert J. Miller.
He grants what the laws of Leviticus 21 and Deuteronomy 22 require, and denies
that the word in them means "virgin": "As in other Greek literature, parthenos
in the Septuagint did not by itself connote what we mean by virginity", so that
the virginity "has to be inferred from the context" (*Born Divine*). The
question to ask of any such dissent is this: **does it still stand once the
texts it cites are read?**

## His evidence, read

Miller gives two uses of the word of a woman who is not a virgin.

- **Joel 1:8**, "Lament like a parthenos dressed in sackcloth for the husband of
  her youth", a young widow. The Greek does not read so: it calls the woman
  νύμφην, a bride, and its παρθεν- word, τὸν παρθενικόν, is of the husband
  (Rahlfs). The text refutes the claim.
- **Genesis 34:3**: "In one passage, this term refers to a rape victim after she
  has been attacked." The Greek calls Dinah a παρθένος in the verse after
  Shechem lies with her, and that much the text reads. But Miller's claim is
  more: that the noun describes her as she then was, no longer a virgin, so that
  it is not used there in the sense "virgin". That is his premise, not the
  text's. The order of the verses puts Shechem's love after his act; it does not
  put the noun's description there. A noun is read at a time of its own, which
  the context gives (Enç 1986): Scripture names Rahab "the harlot" long after
  Jericho (Hebrews 11:31). The status reading takes the noun as the law's name
  for the woman a man has lain with (`dinahLine`).

## What the checks find

The library strikes a claim only when a reading of a text refutes it — Scripture,
rated `consensus` — and then runs every check on what is left
(`Testimony.Logic.Credibility`). Struck of Joel 1:8, Miller's dissent is his
case from Genesis 34:3 (`miller_struck_is_his_case_from_genesis`), and it still
denies the laws' step, granting the laws' grounds. His premise about the noun is
not struck: no text reads otherwise, and an argument strikes nothing. It is
weighed instead.

- **Under the evidence and tradition standards** his dissent is a credible
  critique. His premise rests on argued scholarship, which both standards
  admit.
- **Under the Scripture standard** it is not
  (`miller_survives_on_genesis`). The laws' grounds are all Scripture, and a
  dissent from such a step must rest on Scripture alone. What the Greek of
  34:3 reads is Scripture; that its noun describes Dinah as she then was is
  Miller's reading of it.
- **His denial needs that premise** (`miller_rests_on_the_noun`). Grant what the
  Greek reads and every step of his, and the laws' sense can still stand.

Had Joel 1:8 been all his evidence, the dissent would not count under any
standard: struck of it, nothing in it would deny the step
(`miller_on_joel_alone_does_not_count`). That is the rule at work: evidence the
texts refute stops counting, and a dissent that needed it stops counting with it.

## Weighed in the dispute, and overruled

A credible dissent can still lose when it is weighed. In the dispute above,
Miller's case from Genesis 34:3 is a party, beside Wegner's, and the solver
computes that nothing can defend it (`miller_indefensible`). The status reading
concludes that the word names Dinah in the sense "virgin", which Miller's
premise and his thesis deny; he attacks it back, and fails, because his step,
rated `disputed`, is weaker than the status reading's, rated `plausible`.
Nothing answers the status reading, so nothing defends Miller.

A dissent overruled so stops counting against the step
(`Testimony.Logic.Credibility`, `Overruled`), on one condition, which keeps the
rule from arguing in a circle: the dispute must weigh the step at its floor. It
does. The case from the laws cites its step `disputed` there, so Miller is
overruled with the laws at their weakest, and the overruling owes nothing to the
rating it lets stand.

So the laws' step stands at its cited `wellSupported` under every standard
(`laws_step_ratings`): under the evidence and tradition standards because the
one credible dissent is overruled, and under the Scripture standard because it
is not heard. The verdict turns, as the dispute's does, on the status reading's
step, rated `plausible`. Rated `disputed`, it would not outrank Miller, he would
stand off with it, and his dissent would count again.


## How this is checked

<details class="testimony-checked">
<summary>The positions, steps and results behind this chapter, each with the formula or the Lean that checks it</summary>

##### The Septuagint as a witness

Each reading below is a model: a way every claim of the argument could stand at
once, named for what it says of the Septuagint and of the woman of 7:14. It
settles those as its namesake does. Where the argument's joins require a side on
questions this module does not touch, it takes the scriptural reading's: that
Micah's mention of a mother and no father does mean something, and that
Scripture, not the magisterium, is the judge. Every other claim it leaves true,
and none of them bears on the results it is used for.

<a id="virginConceivesReading"></a>
**`virginConceivesReading`**

Justin's reading of the elders' Greek, with Rico and Gentry's sense of the
word: παρθένος means a virgin, the translator read the woman of 7:14 as one, and
she conceives as one — "a sign which is not common to all the first-born sons"
(*Dialogue* 84). So she is not already pregnant when the sign is given, and her
pregnancy is no ordinary one. Wegner's claim is false in it: the word already
had the sense "virgin". So are Miller's thesis and his premise that the noun of
Genesis 34:3 describes Dinah as she then was: the noun names her.

```lean
def virginConceivesReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.parthenosDoesNotItselfConnoteVirginity => False
    | Claim.parthenosDescribesDinahAsSheThenWas => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="archaismReading"></a>
**`archaismReading`**

Rico and Gentry's reading of Genesis 34:3: the word there is said of Dinah
as she then was, no longer a virgin, an archaism of the Greek Pentateuch, "the
exception that proves the rule" (21); and in the Septuagint at large it means a
virgin. So the verse uses the word otherwise, and the status reading is false
in it; Wegner's claim is false too. Otherwise as Justin reads the elders' Greek
(`virginConceivesReading`).

```lean
def archaismReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.parthenosDoesNotItselfConnoteVirginity => False
    | Claim.dinahIsTheLawsParthenos => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.pregnancyAtTheSignIsOrdinary => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagintWitness_establishes"></a>
**`septuagintWitness_establishes`**

**The Septuagint, read with Rico and Gentry, is a witness from before
Christ.** Grant that the Greek Isaiah renders עַלְמָה with παρθένος, that it was
made by Jews before Christ, and that παρθένος in its Greek means a virgin, and
it follows that a Jewish translator, before Christ, read the woman of 7:14 as a
virgin.

That is the whole of what it delivers: a claim about how the first translator
read the verse. It does not show that παρθένος meant "virgin" in the
translator's day: that is granted here, and rated `disputed`
(`parthenos_is_load_bearing`). Nor does it show what עַלְמָה means
(`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`), or how the woman conceived
(`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`).

```lean
theorem septuagintWitness_establishes : Establishes septuagintWitness
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable`**

The Septuagint as a witness has a model.

```lean
theorem septuagintWitness_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    septuagintWitness.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="wegnerDriftReading"></a>
**`wegnerDriftReading`**

Wegner's reading: in the translator's day παρθένος meant "young woman", with
or without virginity, and did not yet mean "virgin"; so the Greek does not show
that its translator read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin, nor anything about how
she conceived, and עַלְמָה does not denote a virgin either. The woman of 7:14 is
already pregnant when the sign is given, and the sign need not be a miracle.
Wegner does not take up the laws of the Greek Pentateuch. This reading extends
his view to them as Miller reads them: the laws say what they say, and the word
in them still means "young woman". Nor does he take up Exodus 22:15–16; in this
reading Genesis 34 is told in that law's words, and Dinah is still called a
παρθένος in the older sense.

```lean
def wegnerDriftReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | Claim.dinahIsTheLawsParthenos => False
    | Claim.lxxIsaiahUsesParthenosAsVirgin => False
    | Claim.lxxReadsAVirgin => False
    | Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception => False
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.signMustBeExtraordinary => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parthenos_is_load_bearing"></a>
**`parthenos_is_load_bearing`**

**The word carries the whole witness.** Keep the rendering and its date —
the Greek has παρθένος, and Jews made it before Christ — and grant nothing about
what παρθένος meant to them, and the Septuagint no longer shows that its
translator read the woman as a virgin. On Wegner's reading the word was the
ordinary one for a young woman of marriageable age.

So whoever argues from the Septuagint has to win the claim about the word. Its
date, which the rival grants, does not help without it.

```lean
theorem parthenos_is_load_bearing : ¬Establishes septuagintWithoutTheSense
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### From the translator's reading to Isaiah's word

<a id="septuagintOnTheWord_establishes"></a>
**`septuagintOnTheWord_establishes`**

Add the step from the translator's reading to Isaiah's word, rated
`disputed`, and the case concludes that עַלְמָה denotes a virgin. It is only as
good as that step.

```lean
theorem septuagintOnTheWord_establishes : Establishes septuagintOnTheWord
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable`**

The Septuagint asked for Isaiah's word has a model.

```lean
theorem septuagintOnTheWord_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    septuagintOnTheWord.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="translatorDescribesTheWomanReading"></a>
**`translatorDescribesTheWomanReading`**

The referential reading of the Septuagint: its translator read the woman of
7:14 as a virgin, with a word that means one, and עַלְמָה still denotes only a
young woman of marriageable age. He described the woman, not the word, and the
woman is a virgin.

```lean
def translatorDescribesTheWomanReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.parthenosDoesNotItselfConnoteVirginity => False
    | Claim.parthenosDescribesDinahAsSheThenWas => False
    | Claim.almahMeansVirgin => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference`**

**The Septuagint shows how its translator read the woman, not what Isaiah's
word means.** Grant everything the witness rests on, παρθένος as "virgin"
included, and grant that the translator read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin:
עַלְמָה can still denote only a young woman, as the referential strand reads it.
The step from the one to the other is the weight, and it is rated `disputed`:
Bratcher and Brown grant that the translator read the woman as a virgin and deny
that עַלְמָה says so, and Walton holds that the Greek shows "at best ... an
interpretational preference rather than a linguistic necessity" (293). On
Bratcher's reading (113), the Septuagint's translators render the woman, not the
word: παρθένος for Rebekah, whom the story calls a virgin (Genesis 24:43), and
νεᾶνις at Exodus 2:8, Psalm 67:26 (68:25 in English Bibles), Song 1:3 and 6:8.
Jerome reads Rebekah the other way, as showing that עַלְמָה denotes a virgin
(*Against Jovinianus* I.32).

So the Septuagint cannot by itself settle the claim that עַלְמָה itself denotes a
virgin, however its word is read. If its word means "virgin", what it can do is
what the referential strand already needs: show that a virgin answers the
description.

```lean
theorem septuagint_word_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails
    septuagintLine.premises (p Claim.almahMeansVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### What the Greek leaves open

<a id="nowAVirginReading"></a>
**`nowAVirginReading`**

Bratcher's reading of the Greek, who holds that its word means a virgin: "a
young woman, at that time virgin, would in the normal way marry and bear a
child" (115). Rhodea gives the Greek the same reading, granting its sense for
argument's sake and quoting Tsevat: "The pregnancy lies in the future ...;
nothing indicates that the woman is also a virgin after the conception" (67).
The word means a virgin, the translator read her as one, and she is one when the
sign is given; she conceives later, by a man.

```lean
def nowAVirginReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman => False
    | Claim.parthenosDoesNotItselfConnoteVirginity => False
    | Claim.parthenosDescribesDinahAsSheThenWas => False
    | Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception => False
    | Claim.harahIsPredicateAdjective => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsAlreadyPregnant => False
    | Claim.isaianicAlmahIsNotAVirgin => False
    | Claim.maternalSilenceProvesNothing => False
    | Claim.magisteriumIsDoctrinallyAuthoritative => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open"></a>
**`septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open`**

**Granted every word, the Septuagint leaves the conception open.** Keep the
rendering, its date, παρθένος as "virgin", the reading it delivers, and the tense
of the verb — the virgin *shall* be with child — and whether its translator
meant a conception without a man is independent of all of it. On Bratcher's
reading, who holds that the word means a virgin, she is a virgin when the sign is
given and later conceives in the ordinary way; Rhodea reads it so too, granting
the sense for argument's sake. On Justin's she conceives as a virgin. Both
readings keep every premise.

No premise here speaks to how she conceives, so the result says only that the
Greek's own words leave it open. Justin's argument that an ordinary conception
would be no sign is the sign argument's, and is weighed in `Dispute.Wegner`.

The result has two halves: the Greek does not show that the translator meant a
conception without a man, and does not show that he did not. If its sense is
granted, the Septuagint's word answers the objection that the virgin reading was
a Christian invention; it does not supply the virginal conception. That comes, if
it comes, from the promise of a sign (`signLine`), or from Matthew and Luke.

```lean
theorem septuagint_leaves_the_conception_open : Independent
    septuagintWithTheFuture.premises (p Claim.lxxEnvisagesAVirginalConception)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Wegner and Rico and Gentry as positions

<a id="driftObjection_establishes"></a>
**`driftObjection_establishes`**

Wegner on παρθένος delivers its conclusion.

```lean
theorem driftObjection_establishes : Establishes driftObjection
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="driftObjection_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`driftObjection_is_satisfiable`**

Wegner on παρθένος has a model: his own reading, in which the word had not
yet come to mean "virgin".

```lean
theorem driftObjection_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable driftObjection.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="drift_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`drift_rests_on_its_inference`**

**Wegner on παρθένος rests on its inference.** On Rico and Gentry's reading
all three grounds are granted: the older Greek usage, the Greek's παρθένος at
Genesis 34:3, and that the noun there describes Dinah as she then was, no longer
a virgin. And the word still means a virgin in the Septuagint at large: the verse
is an archaism of the Greek Pentateuch. The grounds do not decide the question;
the step does, and that is why it is rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem drift_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails driftLine.grounds (p
    Claim.parthenosMeantYoungWoman)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="usageCase_establishes"></a>
**`usageCase_establishes`**

Rico and Gentry's case delivers its conclusion.

```lean
theorem usageCase_establishes : Establishes usageCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="usageCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`usageCase_is_satisfiable`**

Rico and Gentry's case has a model: Justin's reading of the elders' Greek.

```lean
theorem usageCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable usageCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="usage_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`usage_rests_on_its_inference`**

**Rico and Gentry's case rests on its inference.** On the reading Davidson
(1899, 456) and Meade (2013) give, Trypho objects to παρθένος and the Three
write νεᾶνις because by then Christians had put the sense "virgin" on the word,
while in the translator's day it still meant a young woman; and the Greek
Isaiah's other παρθένοι still render בְּתוּלָה. The countermodel is Wegner's
reading, which allows all of this. The grounds do not decide the question; the
step does, and that is why it is rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem usage_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails usageLine.grounds (p
    Claim.parthenosMeansVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lawsCase_establishes"></a>
**`lawsCase_establishes`**

The case from the laws delivers its conclusion.

```lean
theorem lawsCase_establishes : Establishes lawsCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="lawsCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`lawsCase_is_satisfiable`**

The case from the laws has a model: the reading Justin gives the elders'
Greek, extended to the laws. "Virgin" is a sense of the word, and the laws use
it so.

```lean
theorem lawsCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable lawsCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="laws_rest_on_their_inference"></a>
**`laws_rest_on_their_inference`**

**The case from the laws rests on its inference.** The high priest's
παρθένος is set against the widow and the harlot, and the bride without τὰ
παρθένια dies as a harlot; and still, on Miller's reading, which Wegner's thesis
requires, the word itself means a young woman there, as at Genesis 34:3. What the
laws read does not decide the word's sense; the step does, and its rating is one
of the four that would decide the dispute.

```lean
theorem laws_rest_on_their_inference : ¬Entails lawsLine.grounds (p
    Claim.lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="dinahCase_establishes"></a>
**`dinahCase_establishes`**

The status reading delivers its conclusion.

```lean
theorem dinahCase_establishes : Establishes dinahCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="dinahCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`dinahCase_is_satisfiable`**

The status reading has a model: the reading Justin gives the elders' Greek,
extended to Genesis 34. "Virgin" is a sense of the word, and Dinah is called by
it.

```lean
theorem dinahCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable dinahCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="dinah_rests_on_its_inference"></a>
**`dinah_rests_on_its_inference`**

**The status reading rests on its inference.** Grant what Exodus 22:15–16
reads, and that Genesis 34 tells Shechem's act in the words of the laws: on
Wegner's reading, which Rico and Gentry share for this verse, the Greek still
calls Dinah a παρθένος in the older sense, "young woman", and not as the law's
virgin. The texts do not decide which; the step does, and that is why it is
rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem dinah_rests_on_its_inference : ¬Entails dinahLine.grounds (p
    Claim.dinahIsTheLawsParthenos)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="millerCase_establishes"></a>
**`millerCase_establishes`**

Miller from Genesis 34:3 delivers his conclusion.

```lean
theorem millerCase_establishes : Establishes millerCase
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="millerCase_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`millerCase_is_satisfiable`**

Miller from Genesis 34:3 has a model: Wegner's reading, which takes the
laws as Miller reads them, and the noun at 34:3 as said of Dinah as she then
was.

```lean
theorem millerCase_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable millerCase.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Strength

<a id="septuagintWitness_strength"></a>
**`septuagintWitness_strength`**

The witness is no stronger than its claim about the word, cited
`disputed`. Its step is rated `plausible`, and does not lower it further.

```lean
theorem septuagintWitness_strength : septuagintWitness.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="driftObjection_strength"></a>
**`driftObjection_strength`**

Wegner's grounds are well supported and `consensus`, but his inference is
`disputed`, on Rico and Gentry and on Bratcher.

```lean
theorem driftObjection_strength : driftObjection.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="usageCase_strength"></a>
**`usageCase_strength`**

Rico and Gentry's grounds are `consensus`, but their inference is
`disputed`, on Davidson and Meade.

```lean
theorem usageCase_strength : usageCase.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="millerCase_strength"></a>
**`millerCase_strength`**

Miller's grounds are `consensus`, what the Greek reads, and `wellSupported`,
his premise about the noun; but his inference is `disputed`, on Rico and Gentry
and on Bratcher, who grant both and hold the word means "virgin".

```lean
theorem millerCase_strength : millerCase.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="lawsCase_strength"></a>
**`lawsCase_strength`**

The laws' grounds are `consensus`, what the Greek reads, but their inference
is `disputed`, on Miller.

```lean
theorem lawsCase_strength : lawsCase.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="dinahCase_strength"></a>
**`dinahCase_strength`**

The status reading's grounds are `consensus`, what the texts read, and its
inference is `plausible`: no cited reader grants the law's words in Genesis 34
and denies it, and none has been found who argues it.

```lean
theorem dinahCase_strength : dinahCase.strength = 1
-- axioms: propext
```

#### The defeats

<a id="drift_defeats_septuagint"></a>
**`drift_defeats_septuagint`**

**Wegner defeats the Septuagint's witness.** What he holds — his conclusion,
with what it means — denies the witness's ground that παρθένος means a virgin,
which, cited `disputed`, does not outrank him.

```lean
theorem drift_defeats_septuagint : Defeats driftObjection septuagintWitness
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagint_defeats_drift"></a>
**`septuagint_defeats_drift`**

**The witness defeats Wegner back**, so the two stand off. It holds that the
word means a virgin, which denies what Wegner concludes, and he is no stronger
than it.

```lean
theorem septuagint_defeats_drift : Defeats septuagintWitness driftObjection
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="drift_defeats_usage"></a>
**`drift_defeats_usage`**

**Wegner defeats Rico and Gentry.** His conclusion denies theirs.

```lean
theorem drift_defeats_usage : Defeats driftObjection usageCase
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="usage_defeats_drift"></a>
**`usage_defeats_drift`**

**Rico and Gentry defeat Wegner.** Their conclusion denies his.

```lean
theorem usage_defeats_drift : Defeats usageCase driftObjection
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="drift_defeats_laws"></a>
**`drift_defeats_laws`**

**Wegner defeats the case from the laws.** That the word had not yet come to
mean "virgin" excludes that the laws used it in that sense, because a sense the
word has in one passage of the Septuagint is a sense of the Septuagint's Greek.
The laws, at `disputed`, are no stronger than he.

```lean
theorem drift_defeats_laws : Defeats driftObjection lawsCase
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="laws_defeats_drift"></a>
**`laws_defeats_drift`**

**The case from the laws defeats Wegner.** Their sense "virgin" excludes his
"not yet 'virgin'", and he is no stronger than they.

```lean
theorem laws_defeats_drift : Defeats lawsCase driftObjection
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="drift_does_not_defeat_dinah"></a>
**`drift_does_not_defeat_dinah`**

**Wegner does not defeat the status reading.** That the word had not yet
come to mean "virgin" excludes that Genesis 34:3 uses it in that sense, by the
same definition, so he attacks it. But a rebuttal succeeds only if the attacker
is no weaker than the attacked, and Wegner, whose step is `disputed`, is weaker
than the status reading, whose step is `plausible`.

```lean
theorem drift_does_not_defeat_dinah : ¬Defeats driftObjection dinahCase
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="dinah_defeats_drift"></a>
**`dinah_defeats_drift`**

**The status reading defeats Wegner.** Its sense "virgin" at Genesis 34:3
excludes his "not yet 'virgin'", and he is no stronger than it.

```lean
theorem dinah_defeats_drift : Defeats dinahCase driftObjection
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

#### The dispute

<a id="septuagintPartyNode"></a>
**`septuagintPartyNode`**

The package each party argues from.

```lean
def septuagintPartyNode : SeptuagintParty → ArgumentPackage Claim :=
  fun x =>
    match x with
    | SeptuagintParty.witness => septuagintWitness
    | SeptuagintParty.drift => driftObjection
    | SeptuagintParty.usage => usageCase
    | SeptuagintParty.laws => lawsCase
    | SeptuagintParty.dinah => dinahCase
    | SeptuagintParty.miller => millerCase
```

<a id="septuagintDispute"></a>
**`septuagintDispute`**

The dispute over the Septuagint's word: every party's premises have a model,
every party establishes its conclusion, and every party's inferences are
rated. Each party's weakest link is at the bottom, but the status reading's,
one step up.

```lean
def septuagintDispute : Dispute Claim SeptuagintParty :=
  { node := septuagintPartyNode,
    consistent := septuagintDispute._proof_1,
    sound := septuagintDispute._proof_2,
    rated := septuagintDispute._proof_9 }
```

<a id="septuagintDispute_defeats"></a>
**`septuagintDispute_defeats`**

**Who defeats whom**, all thirty-six pairs: Wegner defeats the witness,
Rico and Gentry and the laws, and each defeats him back; so does Miller, and
each defeats him back; the status reading defeats Wegner and Miller, and
neither defeats it; and nothing else. Every cell is computed from what the
parties hold by `Horn.defeats?` and checked by the kernel.

```lean
theorem septuagintDispute_defeats : ∀ (i j : SeptuagintParty),
    septuagintDispute.defeats i j ↔ (i, j) ∈ [(SeptuagintParty.drift,
    SeptuagintParty.witness), (SeptuagintParty.witness,
    SeptuagintParty.drift), (SeptuagintParty.drift, SeptuagintParty.usage),
    (SeptuagintParty.usage, SeptuagintParty.drift), (SeptuagintParty.drift,
    SeptuagintParty.laws), (SeptuagintParty.laws, SeptuagintParty.drift),
    (SeptuagintParty.dinah, SeptuagintParty.drift), (SeptuagintParty.miller,
    SeptuagintParty.witness), (SeptuagintParty.witness,
    SeptuagintParty.miller), (SeptuagintParty.miller, SeptuagintParty.usage),
    (SeptuagintParty.usage, SeptuagintParty.miller), (SeptuagintParty.miller,
    SeptuagintParty.laws), (SeptuagintParty.laws, SeptuagintParty.miller),
    (SeptuagintParty.dinah, SeptuagintParty.miller)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintDispute_supports"></a>
**`septuagintDispute_supports`**

**One support**, in all thirty-six pairs: Rico and Gentry's conclusion is the
witness's contested ground, that "virgin" is a sense of παρθένος. The library
draws a support only where one party's conclusion is, word for word, another's
premise. The laws and the status reading reach the witness's ground through a
definition, so no support is drawn from them, though they lead to the same
ground. Every cell is computed
by `supports?` and checked by the kernel.

```lean
theorem septuagintDispute_supports : ∀ (i j : SeptuagintParty),
    septuagintDispute.supports i j ↔ (i, j) ∈ [(SeptuagintParty.usage,
    SeptuagintParty.witness)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintDispute_partOf"></a>
**`septuagintDispute_partOf`**

**No case is part of another's** here, in all thirty-six pairs, except each
party's own. Every cell is computed by `partOf?` and checked by the kernel.

```lean
theorem septuagintDispute_partOf : ∀ (i j : SeptuagintParty),
    septuagintDispute.partOf i j ↔ i = j ∨ (i, j) ∈ []
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagint_stands_with_the_usage"></a>
**`septuagint_stands_with_the_usage`**

**The witness, Rico and Gentry, the laws and the status reading stand
together**, on the reading Justin gives the elders' Greek, extended to the
Pentateuch: "virgin" is a sense of the word, the laws use it so, Genesis 34:3
names Dinah by it, and the translator read the woman of 7:14 as a virgin.

```lean
theorem septuagint_stands_with_the_usage : septuagintDispute.StandTogether
    [SeptuagintParty.witness, SeptuagintParty.usage, SeptuagintParty.laws,
    SeptuagintParty.dinah]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagintHeardInStages"></a>
**`septuagintHeardInStages`**

Why the Septuagint's side prevails, in stages: the status reading first,
which nothing defeats; then the witness, Rico and Gentry and the laws, whom it
defends by defeating Wegner and Miller; and Wegner and Miller out, each defeated
by the status reading.

**What the dispute forces is exactly *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16*, *The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)*, *Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures*, *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*.**

- Stage 1: *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16*.
  - *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* is defeated by nothing.
- Stage 2: *The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)*, *Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures*, *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*.
  - *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'* defeats *The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'*.
  - *Miller, from Genesis 34:3* defeats *The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Miller, from Genesis 34:3*.
  - *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'* defeats *Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'*.
  - *Miller, from Genesis 34:3* defeats *Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Miller, from Genesis 34:3*.
  - *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'* defeats *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'*.
  - *Miller, from Genesis 34:3* defeats *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*, and *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Miller, from Genesis 34:3*.
- Nothing else is forced:
  - *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'*, and nothing forced defeats *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16*.
  - *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16* defeats *Miller, from Genesis 34:3*, and nothing forced defeats *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 8 defeats and 18 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`septuagintDispute_defeats`](#septuagintDispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *The Septuagint as a witness (Isaiah 7:14 in Greek)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - In the Greek of the Septuagint, παρθένος means a virgin — [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), p. 21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 472
- *The law's name for Dinah: Genesis 34:3 read under Exodus 22:15–16*, weakest at *plausible*:
  - an inference step — Exod 22:15-16; Exod 22:15-16; Gen 34:2; Gen 34:2; Gen 34:7; Gen 34:12; Gen 34:12; Deut 22:29; Deut 22:29; Deut 22:21; [Frymer-Kensky 1998](../../bibliography.md#frymer-kensky-virginity-1998), pp. 80, 91; [Enç 1986](../../bibliography.md#enc-referential-analysis-1986), pp. 405–426; [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), pp. 18–21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113; [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), p. 483; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67
- *Wegner on παρθένος: the word had not yet come to mean 'virgin'*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - an inference step — [Wegner 2011](../../bibliography.md#wegner-virgin-births-2011), pp. 482–483; [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67; [Meade 2013](../../bibliography.md#meade-ancient-versions-comment-2013); [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), pp. 18–21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), pp. 112–113
- *Rico and Gentry: παρθένος means 'virgin' in the Greek of the Scriptures*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - an inference step — [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), p. 21; [Postell 2025](../../bibliography.md#postell-isaiah-messianic-2025), p. 472; [Davidson 1899](../../bibliography.md#davidson-immanuel-1899), p. 456; [Meade 2013](../../bibliography.md#meade-ancient-versions-comment-2013)
- *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - an inference step — [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 102; [Liddell and Scott 1940](../../bibliography.md#liddell-scott-jones-lexicon-1940), p. 1339; [Muraoka 2009](../../bibliography.md#muraoka-lexicon-septuagint-2009), p. 535; [Lust et al. 2003](../../bibliography.md#lust-lexicon-septuagint-2003), s.v. παρθένια; [Miller 2003](../../bibliography.md#miller-born-divine-2003); [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67
- *Miller, from Genesis 34:3*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - an inference step — [Miller 2003](../../bibliography.md#miller-born-divine-2003); [Rico and Gentry 2020](../../bibliography.md#rico-gentry-infant-king-2020), pp. 18–21; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113

<a id="septuagint_prevails_over_wegner"></a>
**`septuagint_prevails_over_wegner`**

**The Septuagint's side prevails, and neither Wegner nor Miller does.**
Nothing defeats the status reading of Genesis 34:3, because Wegner and Miller
are each weaker than it, so it is accepted first. It defeats them both, the only
parties that defeat the witness, Rico and Gentry or the laws, so all three are
accepted with it; and nothing defends either. The verdict turns on one rating,
the status reading's step (`dinahLine`).

```lean
theorem septuagint_prevails_over_wegner : Framework.grounded
    septuagintDispute.defeats = {SeptuagintParty.witness,
    SeptuagintParty.usage, SeptuagintParty.laws, SeptuagintParty.dinah}
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="miller_indefensible"></a>
**`miller_indefensible`**

**Miller from Genesis 34:3 cannot be defended.** No admissible set contains
him: the status reading defeats him, and nothing defeats the status reading. His
case denies what it concludes, that the word names Dinah in the sense "virgin";
he attacks it back, and fails, being the weaker.

```lean
theorem miller_indefensible : ∀ (S : Set SeptuagintParty),
    Framework.Admissible septuagintDispute.defeats S → SeptuagintParty.miller
    ∉ S
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="septuagint_skeptically_accepted"></a>
**`septuagint_skeptically_accepted`**

So every resolution of the dispute accepts the Septuagint's witness.

```lean
theorem septuagint_skeptically_accepted : Framework.SkepticallyAccepted
    septuagintDispute.defeats SeptuagintParty.witness
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="drift_not_credulously_accepted"></a>
**`drift_not_credulously_accepted`**

And none accepts Wegner on παρθένος.

```lean
theorem drift_not_credulously_accepted : ¬Framework.CredulouslyAccepted
    septuagintDispute.defeats SeptuagintParty.drift
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

#### Miller's dissent

<a id="joelReadsABride"></a>
**`joelReadsABride`**

**What the Greek of Joel 1:8 reads**: the woman is νύμφην, a bride, and
τὸν παρθενικόν is said of her husband. A reading of the text, from Rahlfs.

```lean
def joelReadsABride : Refutation Claim :=
  { claim := Claim.joelGreekCallsTheWidowParthenos,
    reads :=
      "the Greek of Joel 1:8 calls the woman νύμφην, a bride; its παρθεν- word, " ++
        "τὸν παρθενικόν, is of the husband",
    reading :=
      {
        primary :=
          Reference.scripture
            [Scripture.verseIn TextualTradition.septuagint
                { book := Book.joel, chapter := 1, verse := 8 }],
        tradition := Tradition.criticalScholarship,
        confidence := Confidence.consensus } }
```

#### Assessed, with what the texts refute struck

<a id="millerOnLawsAssessment"></a>
**`millerOnLawsAssessment`**

**Miller against the laws' step**, with Joel 1:8 struck. Consistent,
granting the laws' grounds, and argued: struck of Joel 1:8, his dissent still
denies the step through Genesis 34:3. What it still asserts outright is the
Greek's reading of the verse, and his premise that its noun describes Dinah as
she then was. The first is Scripture; the second is his reading of it, argued
scholarship. So the dissent is a credible critique under the evidence and
tradition standards. Under the Scripture standard it is not: the laws' grounds
are all Scripture, and his premise is not.

**Dissent:** *Miller, Born Divine*, against *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*. ✔ A critique: it can be held with the step's grounds, and it argues its denial by a step of its own.

- **Struck, because the text reads otherwise:** The Greek of Joel 1:8 calls a young widow a παρθένος (Miller). the Greek of Joel 1:8 calls the woman νύμφην, a bride; its παρθεν- word, τὸν παρθενικόν, is of the husband.

| Standard | A credible critique? | Rests on what the standard does not accept |
|---|---|---|
| evidence | ✔ yes | — |
| tradition | ✔ yes | — |
| Scripture | ✘ no | At 34:3 παρθένος describes Dinah as she then was, no longer a virgin (Miller) |

<a id="miller_struck_is_his_case_from_genesis"></a>
**`miller_struck_is_his_case_from_genesis`**

**Struck of Joel 1:8, Miller's dissent is his case from Genesis 34:3**: with
the claim the Greek refutes taken out, and his step from it, the premises the
checks weigh are, formula for formula, the premises of the position
he holds in the dispute over the Septuagint's word (`millerCase`).

```lean
theorem miller_struck_is_his_case_from_genesis :
    millerOnLawsAssessment.dissent.premises = millerCase.premises
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="miller_survives_on_genesis"></a>
**`miller_survives_on_genesis`**

**Miller survives on Genesis 34:3, and turns on the standard.** Struck of
Joel 1:8, which the Greek refutes, his dissent from the laws' step is still a
credible critique under the evidence and tradition standards: Genesis 34:3
carries his denial. Under the Scripture standard it is not, because it carries
it only with his premise that the noun describes Dinah as she then was, and that
is not Scripture.

```lean
theorem miller_survives_on_genesis : millerOnLawsAssessment.findings.struck =
    [Claim.joelGreekCallsTheWidowParthenos] ∧ Dissent.Credible
    Standard.evidence millerOnLawsAssessment.dissent ∧ Dissent.Credible
    Standard.tradition millerOnLawsAssessment.dissent ∧ ¬Dissent.Credible
    Standard.scriptural millerOnLawsAssessment.dissent
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="miller_rests_on_the_noun"></a>
**`miller_rests_on_the_noun`**

**Miller's denial rests on his premise about the noun.** Grant what the Greek
of Genesis 34:3 reads, and every step of his, and the laws' sense still stands:
on the reading Justin gives the elders' Greek, the noun names Dinah, and the
word is used of her in the sense "virgin". Miller's conclusion needs his further
premise, that the noun describes her as she then was. A noun need not: it is
read at a time of its own (Enç 1986), as Scripture names Rahab "the harlot" long
after Jericho (Hebrews 11:31).

```lean
theorem miller_rests_on_the_noun : ¬Entails (caseOf [millerDinahLine.onGrounds
    [p Claim.greekCallsDinahParthenos]] [] [contextNotWordInTheLaws]) (notP
    Claim.lawsUseParthenosAsVirgin)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="millerOnJoelAloneAssessment"></a>
**`millerOnJoelAloneAssessment`**

**Miller from Joel 1:8 alone**, with Joel 1:8 struck: nothing left denies the
step.

**Dissent:** *Miller, from Joel 1:8 alone*, against *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'*. ✘ Not a critique of this step: with the claims the texts refute struck, what remains does not deny what the step concludes.

- **Struck, because the text reads otherwise:** The Greek of Joel 1:8 calls a young widow a παρθένος (Miller). the Greek of Joel 1:8 calls the woman νύμφην, a bride; its παρθεν- word, τὸν παρθενικόν, is of the husband.

| Standard | A credible critique? | Rests on what the standard does not accept |
|---|---|---|
| evidence | ✘ no | — |
| tradition | ✘ no | — |
| Scripture | ✘ no | — |

<a id="miller_on_joel_alone_does_not_count"></a>
**`miller_on_joel_alone_does_not_count`**

**Evidence the texts refute stops counting.** Had Miller rested his dissent on
Joel 1:8 alone, then, with the claim the Greek refutes struck, nothing in it
would deny the laws' step, and it would not be a credible critique under any
standard.

```lean
theorem miller_on_joel_alone_does_not_count : ∀ (s : Standard),
    ¬Dissent.Credible s millerOnJoelAloneAssessment.dissent
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

#### The laws' step, rated

<a id="lawsStep"></a>
**`lawsStep`**

**The laws' step, rated by its register**: Miller's dissent, the strongest
known, with what the texts refute struck. Its support is cited `wellSupported`:
Bratcher, and the lexica on τὰ παρθένια.

Miller's dissent is overruled in the dispute over the Septuagint's word, where
his case from Genesis 34:3 is a party and nothing defends it
(`miller_indefensible`). That dispute weighs the laws' step at its floor: the
case from the laws cites it `disputed` there. So the overruling owes nothing to
the rating it lets stand.

**The rating, computed.** *The laws of the Greek Pentateuch: παρθένος in the sense 'virgin'* is cited at *well supported* ([Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 113; [Bratcher 1958](../../bibliography.md#bratcher-study-of-isaiah-1958), p. 102; [Liddell and Scott 1940](../../bibliography.md#liddell-scott-jones-lexicon-1940), p. 1339; [Muraoka 2009](../../bibliography.md#muraoka-lexicon-septuagint-2009), p. 535; [Lust et al. 2003](../../bibliography.md#lust-lexicon-septuagint-2003), s.v. παρθένια; [Miller 2003](../../bibliography.md#miller-born-divine-2003); [Rhodea 2013](../../bibliography.md#rhodea-did-matthew-conceive-2013), p. 67). Dissents encoded: *Miller, Born Divine*. The strongest known: *Miller, Born Divine*.

| Standard | Rating | Why |
|---|---|---|
| evidence | **well supported** | a credible critique, overruled: Miller, Born Divine, in the dispute over the Septuagint's word, where nothing defends it, with the step weighed at its floor |
| tradition | **well supported** | a credible critique, overruled: Miller, Born Divine, in the dispute over the Septuagint's word, where nothing defends it, with the step weighed at its floor |
| Scripture | **well supported** | every encoded dissent fails a check, the strongest known among them, so the step's support stands |

<a id="laws_step_ratings"></a>
**`laws_step_ratings`**

**The laws' step stands at `wellSupported` under every standard, and for two
reasons.** Under the evidence and tradition standards Miller's dissent is a
credible critique, and it is overruled: his case from Genesis 34:3 cannot be
defended in the dispute over the Septuagint's word, which weighs the step at its
floor. Under the Scripture standard his dissent is not heard at all, because his
premise about the noun is not Scripture.

```lean
theorem laws_step_ratings : lawsStep.ratings = [(Standard.evidence,
    Computed.overruled ["Miller, Born Divine"] Confidence.wellSupported),
    (Standard.tradition, Computed.overruled ["Miller, Born Divine"]
    Confidence.wellSupported), (Standard.scriptural, Computed.stands
    Confidence.wellSupported)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```
